title: Mr Ken Foxe & Department of Defence
text:
Decision
Mr Ken Foxe & Department of Defence
From
Office of the Commissioner for Environmental Information (OCEI)
Case number: OCE-161681-D8T6P9
Published on 26 June 2026
Background
Scope of Review
Preliminary Matters
Analysis and Findings
Decision
Appeal to the High Court
Whether the Department was justified in refusing access to information relating to air taxi services hired by the Department on behalf of the President in 2023, 2024, and 2025 under the AIE Regulations.
25 June 2026
Background
1. On 3 July 2025, the appellant submitted a request to the Department, seeking access to: “a record/spreadsheet/database of all air taxi services hired by the department on behalf of the President in 2023, 2024, 2025 to include the date, minute time on board, the route, the department, the number of passengers, and the cost of the service.”
2. The appellant also included the following comments: “I note in the recent FOI decision that reference was made to the Supreme Court judgment concerning the President. However, the Supreme Court judgment has absolutely no bearing on public authorities apart from the President's Office and the Council of State. It does not have any crossover whatsoever to the Department of Defence, against which legal action can be taken. This has already been decided upon by the CEI in previous decisions concerning the use of the Gulfstream jet, which were accepted by the Department of Defence and not appealed to the High Court.”
3. On 5 August 2025, the Department issued its decision, refusing the appellant’s request. It included the following summary of its decision, “[t]his decision is primarily based on the definitive ruling of the Supreme Court ([2022] IESC 19) which affirmed the constitutional immunity of the President for information, including those made under AIE Regulations, irrespective of which public body might hold the information.”
4. The Department also commented “In accordance with Article 10(3) and 10(4) I have weighed the public interest served by disclosure against the interest served by refusal of your request. I have determined that the interest served by refusal outweighs the public interest in disclosure.”
5. However, the Department also went on to acknowledge the Commissioner’s previous decision (CEI/16/0041) which concerned a request for environmental information related to flights undertaken by the Ministerial Air Transport Service, specifically those involving the President. The Department stated that in that case the Commissioner found that the Department of Defence was obliged to disclose environmental information relating to the President's flights and the reasoning underpinning that decision was that Article 3(2) of the AIE Regulations (which excludes certain bodies from the definition of "public authority") did not apply to the Department of Defence.
6. The Department stated “This meant that even if the information related to the President, the Department, as a public authority, still had an obligation to process the AIE request. The OCEI held that information on the dates of travel, departure point and destination, flying time, and the number of passengers is environmental information.”
The Department submitted, however, that decision predates and was fundamentally impacted by the judgment of the Supreme Court of April 29, 2022 which “definitely clarified the scope of the President’s constitutional immunity under Article 13.8.1 of the Constitution of Ireland.”
7. The Department’s view is that the Supreme Court judgment “effectively overruled the interpretation presented in CEI/16/0041 concerning the President’s immunity in the context of AIE Requests”,
establishing that the President’s constitutional immunity extends to AIE requests, the President’s Office is not a “public authority” under AIE, and any attempt to obtain information that would effectively make the President “answerable to the courts”, even if held by another public authority, is precluded by the Constitution. The Department concluded: “In light of the binding precedent set by the Supreme Court, I have concluded that the disclosure of information related to the President’s official acts and functions, as sought in your request, would be contrary to the public interest and would undermine the constitutional immunity afforded to the President.”
8. Also on 5 August 2025, the appellant sought an internal review of that decision. The appellant submitted “The Supreme Court judgment has no application outside of the President, the Secretary General to the President, and the Council of State. It does none of the things described in your decision letter which is based on a misunderstanding of the extent of the judgment. The decision is not supported by any extracts from the judgment, nor could it be, because the judgment does not touch on the issue of records held by other public bodies as in this case.”
9. On 19 August 2025, the Department issued its internal review decision, affirming its original decision. It reiterated that it was refusing access to the information sought on the grounds of the Supreme Court ruling. It stated that it was satisfied that “the constitutional immunity of the President prevents this Department from releasing, under the AIE Regulations, information concerning air travel arranged, on request, on behalf of the President.”
10. On 20 August 2025, the appellant submitted an appeal to this Office of the Department’s decision. He cited the Commissioner’s previous decision in CEI/16/0041 and noted his assertion that the Department “is misinterpreting the recent Supreme Court judgment, which has no application outside of the Office of the President and the Council of State.”
11. I have carried out a review under article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations. In so doing, I have had regard to the correspondence between the Department and the appellant as outlined above and to correspondence between my Office and both the Department and the appellant on the matter. I have also considered a sample of the information sought. In addition, I have had regard to:
• the Guidance document provided by the Minister for the Environment, Community and Local Government on the implementation of the AIE Regulations (the Minister’s Guidance);
• Directive 2003/4/EC (the AIE Directive), upon which the AIE Regulations are based;
• the 1998 United Nations Economic Commission for Europe Convention on Access to Information, Public Participation in Decision-Making and Access to Justice in Environmental Matters (the Aarhus Convention); and
• The Aarhus Convention—An Implementation Guide (Second edition, June 2014) (the Aarhus Guide)
• Right to Know CLG v Commissioner for Environmental Information and others [2022] IESC 19 ] (“the President case”)
12. What follows does not comment or make findings on each and every argument advanced but all relevant points have been considered.
Scope of Review
13. In accordance with article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations, my role is to review the public authority’s internal review decision and to affirm, annul or vary it. Where appropriate in the circumstances of an appeal, I will require the public authority to make available environmental information to the appellant.
14. A review by this Office is considered to be de novo, which means that it is based on the circumstances and the law as they pertain at the time of this decision.
15. It is clear from the comments of the Court of Appeal in Redmond & Another v Commissioner for Environmental Information & Another
[2020
IECA 83 ] , at paragraph 51, that the nature of a review by this Office is inquisitorial, rather than adversarial in nature. The extent of the inquiry is determined by this Office and not by the parties to the appeal.
16. In its original and internal review decisions, the Department refused access to the information sought on the grounds of the Supreme Court ruling the President
case and the “constitutional immunity of the President”
. It was not entirely clear from the Department’s original decision or its internal review decision which provisions of the AIE Regulations were being relied upon to refuse the information. This is unsatisfactory.
17. The Department has since clarified its position in its submissions to this Office, which stated that it was relying on article 3(2) of the AIE Regulations to refuse access on the basis that the request is seeking information indirectly from the President, who is not a public authority (I understand the Department’s view to be that this means that the Department is not a public authority in respect of the request), in addition to relying on exemptions under articles 8(a)(ii) and 9(1)(a) of the AIE Regulations.
18. The Investigator informed the appellant that the Commissioner conducts a fresh review of all aspects of an appeal and is not bound to follow his previous decisions. She summarised and invited the appellant to respond to the Department’s submissions, in particular those that she considered were relevant to the assessment of 9(1)(a) of the AIE Regulations.
19. In the circumstances, I am satisfied the scope of this review concerns whether the Department was justified in refusing access to information relating to air taxi services hired by the Department on behalf of the President in 2023, 2024, and 2025 under the AIE Regulations, on the basis that it is not a public authority in respect of the request and/or on the basis of article 8(a)(ii) or 9(1)(a) of the AIE Regulations.
Preliminary Matters
20. The appellant has referred to the prior decision of this Office in CEI/16/0041
Right to Know CLG and Department of Defence
, in which my predecessor decided that the Department was a public authority in respect of the same type of information. He found that the information requested was held by the Department within the meaning of the AIE Regulations and that refusal of access to the information in that case was not justified under articles 8(a)(i), 8(a)(ii) or 9(1)(a) of the AIE Regulations. That case considered a request to the Department for "a spreadsheet of all travel undertaken by the Ministerial Air Transport Service - to include flights by any aircraft (government jet, Learjet, Beechcraft, Air Corps helicopters etc) - relating (only) to travel by the Presidents Mary McAleese and Michael D Higgins in the period 11 November 1997 to the [date of the request].”
The appellant submits that the matter was fully dealt with in that case and that this appeal should be determined on the same basis. In this regard the appellant has requested that “[g]iven this matter has already been decided by the CEI, I would request that it is dealt with quickly”.
21. I accept that I have a general obligation to act consistently by treating like cases alike, unless there is good reason for not doing so. As will be clear from my decision below, while I continue to be satisfied that the Department is a public authority in relation to the request, I now accept that the Department’s refusal is justified under article 9(1)(a) of the AIE Regulations. Where I propose to reach a different conclusion on a later case in respect of the same or similar issues, I am obliged to make clear the reasons and considerations upon which that change of stance has been adopted.
22. My predecessor’s decision in CEI/16/0041 was made on 30 May 2019, 3 years before the decision of the Supreme Court in the President case. While the Supreme Court dealt specifically with whether the President, the Secretary General to the President and the Council of State were public authorities, the Court’s judgment was extensive and dealt with a number of points of principle that leave the basis of the decision in CEI/16/0041 open to question. For example, in assessing the potential impact of presidential immunity on the AIE regime, my predecessor stated in CEI/16/0041: “It is not clear to me that the President’s immunity under Article 13.8.1° of the Constitution precludes the President, or another entity representing the President’s interests, from electing to participate in proceedings which may arise from the decision in this review.”
It is now clear that this statement was incorrect, as the Supreme Court specifically found that the President is precluded from electing to participate in proceedings. The Court stated at paragraph 116 that “the immunity operates not merely as a privilege conferred on the President, but also as a limitation on the court or the legislature engaging in acts of scrutiny. The presidential immunity precludes the President making a choice to submit to the Commissioner …”
23. Taking this into account, and noting the extensive guidance provided by the Supreme Court in the President case, I consider that I am obliged to carry out my analysis afresh, taking into account all of the Court’s guidance. To the extent that this fresh review gives rise to an inconsistency with a previous decision of this Office, I accept that the previous decision can no longer be considered to be correct.
Analysis and Findings
Whether the Department is a public authority in respect of the request
24. Article 2(2) of the AIE Directive provides:
“‘Public authority’ shall mean:
(a) government or other public administration, including public advisory bodies, at national, regional or local level;
(b) any natural or legal person performing public administrative functions under national law, including specific duties, activities or services in relation to the environment; and
(c) any natural or legal person having public responsibilities or functions, or providing public services, relating to the environment under the control of a body or person falling within (a) or (b).
Member States may provide that this definition shall not include bodies or institutions when acting in a judicial or legislative capacity. If their constitutional provisions at the date of adoption of this Directive make no provision for a review procedure within the meaning of Article 6, Member States may exclude those bodies or institutions from that definition.”
25. Article 3(1) of the AIE Regulations provides:
“’public authority’ means, subject to sub-article (2)—
(a) government or other public administration, including public advisory bodies, at national, regional or local level,
(b) any natural or legal person performing public administrative functions under national law, including specific duties, activities or services in relation to the environment, and
(c) any natural or legal person having public responsibilities or functions, or providing public services, relating to the environment under the control of a body or person falling within paragraph (a) or (b),
and includes – […]”
26. Article 3(2) of the AIE Regulations provides:
“Notwithstanding anything in sub-article (1), in these Regulations “public authority” does not include—
(a) the President,
(b) the Office of the Secretary General to the President,
(c) the Council of State,
(d) any Commission for the time being lawfully exercising the powers and performing the duties of the President, or
(e) any body when acting in a judicial or legislative capacity.”
27. Article 13.8.1 of the Constitution provides “[t]he President shall not be answerable to either House of the Oireachtas or to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers and functions of his office or for any act done or purporting to be done by him in the exercise and performance of these powers and functions.”
28. In the President
case, the Supreme Court held that the President is not a public authority under the AIE Regulations. While the requests were made to the Office of the Secretary General to the President (OSGP) and the Council of State, rather than the President directly, the Court found that the presidential immunity operated to exclude those bodies from the definition of a public authority, so none can be required to answer an AIE request. The Supreme Court reached this conclusion having particular regard to the review and appeal mechanisms under the AIE Regulations. If the President was a public authority, my Office would be empowered to review the decisions of the President and to exercise powers in respect of information, and the courts would be able to review such decisions on appeal, both of which would be fundamentally incompatible with the constitutional provision that the President is not answerable to any Court or to the Oireachtas (see paras 113-119).
29. The Court considered the specific roles of both the OSGP and the Council of State at paragraph 120:
“I return to a proposition, advanced earlier, that the Council of State and the Secretary General to the President assist, advise and counsel the President in the performance of his or her functions and to require either of them to engage with a request from the Commissioner, and thereafter to permit the invocation of court scrutiny of that request by the various means available from the AIE Regulations, would involve scrutiny of an answer by those bodies who act at all times on behalf of the President. The Secretary General to the President cannot be said to hold papers on his or her own personal behalf but does so in the course of assisting the President in the performance of his or her duties. The Council of State equally has no independent existence, and it has the constitutional role of advising and the President at his request to “aid and counsel” the President in the performance of his or her functions. It has no separate or independent function by which it would independently hold information that might be the subject of a request for disclosure.”
30. The Court found that the OSGP had no separate legal personality, meaning the request must be one which in truth was made to the President himself, and it “had the function of seeking to compel the President through his Secretary General to furnish those documents and information”
(paragraph 123). The Court found that the request to the Council of State was “also in substance a request to the President and a request thus framed cannot be entertained, as it has as its effect, or purpose, the circumvention of the presidential immunity” (paragraph 124). The Court stated that the Council of State “is excluded from such requests not because it engages or assists the engagement by the President in a legislative function, but rather because the Council of State is a body that acts under and by the direction of the President and it could not independently hold information nor decide to furnish the information sought.”
(paragraph 128)
31. I have carefully considered whether the same analysis could apply to the Department in this case. It is not in dispute that the Department is generally a public authority. However, I understand the Department’s view to be that it is not a public authority in respect of information held by it that relates to the exercise and performance of the President’s powers and functions. I do not accept this submission, for two related reasons.
32. First, the AIE Directive and Regulations provide a definition of public authority that depends on the nature of the public authority itself
, and not the nature of the information requested
. In most cases, a body is or is not a public authority, based on its status (category (a)), the functions it performs (category (b)), or the control of the body (category (c)). One exception to this is that Member States are permitted to exclude a body which would otherwise be a public authority from the definition when acting in a judicial or legislative capacity, which Ireland has done in article 3(2)(e), but even this relates not to the information held but to the functions being exercised by the body when it created or received that information. It would not be consistent with that overall structure and approach for me to find that the Department’s status as a public authority is dependent on the nature of the information requested
.
33. Second, the Supreme Court in the President case made it clear that its conclusion in relation to the OSGP and the Council of State was based on the inability of either body to hold information independently of the President and the obligation of each body to act under and by the direction of the President. The same cannot be said of the Department in this case. While I accept that the Department holds the requested information on behalf of and to assist the President – and I deal further with the impact of this below – it cannot be said that the Department is incapable of independently holding the information or acting independently of the President’s directions.
34. Taking this into account, I find that the Department is a public authority in relation to the request and that any refusal to provide the information must be based on one or more of the exceptions.
Application of the exceptions
35. The appellant is seeking access to “a record/spreadsheet/database of all air taxi services hired by the department on behalf of the President in 2023, 2024, 2025 to include the date, minute time on board, the route, the department, the number of passengers, and the cost of the service.”
During the course of this review the Department provided this Office with a sample spreadsheet for 2025 containing the relevant information sought.
36. The
Department of Defence and Defence Forces Annual Report 2024
explains that the Ministerial Air Transport Service (MATS) is provided by the Department of Defence to assist the President and members of the Government in fulfilling their official engagements at home and abroad (page 156). There is further detail on the Department’s
website
. The Department explained, in its submissions, the administrative procedure by which the President may make use of MATS:
“Until December 2023, MATS was delivered primarily by the use of the Learjet 45 aircraft, which came into operation in 2004. Where it is unavailable, other suitable Air Corps aircraft may be used. Therefore, in situations where there are no suitable Air Corps aircraft, it has become necessary to avail of an air taxi service. All MATS flights are subject to the approval of the Department of the Taoiseach.
Following approval from the Department of the Taoiseach, the Department of Defence is notified and provided with the necessary flight details. Arrangements are then processed by the Department of Defence, with air taxi costs funded from a contingency framework agreement. The Department of Defence maintains a database in respect of MATs and information in relation to usage of MATS is publicly available on the Department's website, where it is updated on a monthly basis. www.gov.ie/en/organisation-information/e8132-routinely-published-information/#ministerial-air-transport-service-mats”
37. The Department relies on articles 8(a)(ii) and 9(1)(a) to refuse the information requested. These provisions must be read alongside article 10 of the AIE Regulations.
Article 9(1)(a) of the AIE Regulations
Position of the parties
38. In its submissions to this Office the Department contended that the information is exempt under article 9(1)(a) of the AIE Regulations as disclosure would adversely affect national defence and public security. The Department noted that while the information reveals the historic itinerary of the President, this does not render it irrelevant to the prediction of future actions of the President, particularly as it can be combined with other information already available in the public domain. It is also the general thrust of the Department’s position that the disclosure of the information sought would undermine the constitutional immunity afforded to the President.
39. The Department referred to Articles 13.8.1, 13.8.2 and 13.8.3 of the Constitution, as well as section 3 of the Republic of Ireland Act 1948, and submitted that the use of MATS by the President is an act or activity that is necessitated by the performance of the President’s external relations function. The Department stated that the use of MATS is an act done or purporting to be done by [the President] in the exercise and performance of his “powers and functions” and is therefore an act that attracts or is protected by the privilege under the Constitution. The Department stated information requested amounts to details and specifics of the manner in which the President performs his external relations function.
40. The Department submitted that the constitutional position of the President cannot be avoided by seeking information “indirectly” from the Department, rather than directly from the President. The Department noted “it is perfectly clear from the terms of the request that what is sought is information in respect of the Office of President. This is not altered by the fact that the request has been nominally made to the Department of Defence.”
The Department stated that a purpose of the constitutional privilege is to shield the President from an examination of the manner in which he or she performs his or her functions (save by impeachment) so as to keep the Office of the Presidency “above the fray of day to day politics and the allegations and counter allegations that form part of the same”.
41. It noted that this purpose “would be patently set at nought if it could be easily circumvented.”
The Department referred to
section 42(h) of the FOI Act 2014
which “does not simply prohibit requests for information from the President, but, instead excludes records ‘relating to the President’ from its ambit.”
The Department indicated that the type of information sought in this case was previously refused by it in response to an FOI request from the same appellant dated 30 May 2025 under section 42(h) of the FOI Act 2014. I understand that following that decision the appellant submitted the AIE request at issue.
42. The Department submitted that “[w]hile the information that is requested is historical, it is naïve to presume that this renders it irrelevant to the prediction of future actions by the President, particularly as it can be combined with other information already available in the public domain.”
The Department acknowledged that the previous Commissioner’s decision dated 30 May 2019 in
CEI/16/0041
directed the release of certain similar air transport information, however noted that decision predated the findings of the Supreme Court in the President and that the legal landscape has fundamentally changed since CEI/16/0041.
43. In his submissions to this Office, the appellant contended that this matter has already been dealt with by the OCEI and that the reasoning in CEI/16/0041 should be adopted. The appellant disagreed that disclosure of the information sought would jeopardise national security of defence given that the Department publishes such data for the Taoiseach, the Tánaiste, and Ministers at
https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-defence/organisation-information/routinely-published-information/
. The appellant noted that he is aware of the operation of section 42 of the FOI Act 2014, however contended “[t]here is no Section 42 in the AIE Regulations and any court judgment relating to the Office of the President and the Council of State is not relevant to this Request.”
He submitted that he is not using the AIE Regulations “to get around”
the FOI Act and that the AIE Regulations are “the only mechanism the public has to access environmental information in many contexts where the [FOI] Act 2014 is not fit for purpose. This includes dozens of exempt agencies, a very large number of partially included agencies, and scenarios like the one in this case.”
Discussion
44. Article 9(1)(a) of the AIE Regulations provides that a public authority may refuse to make available environmental information where disclosure of the information requested would adversely affect international relations, national defence, or public security. This provision seeks to transpose Article 4(2)(b) of the AIE Directive, which in turn is based on Article 4(4)(b) of the Aarhus Convention. Article 9(1)(a) must be read alongside article 10 of the AIE Regulations. The wording of article 9(1)(a) of the AIE Regulations makes it clear that there must be some adverse effect on public security in order for the exception to apply. There must be a clear link between disclosure of the specific information that it has withheld and any adverse effect. The risk of public security being undermined must be reasonably foreseeable and not purely hypothetical. A mere assertion of an expectation of harm is not sufficient.
45. In summary, the Department submits that the President’s use of MATS is part of the President’s external relations (or international relations) function, but also that disclosure of the information could enable prediction of the future travel arrangements of the President and could place the President at risk. In substance, it seems to me that the Department relies principally on the ‘public security’ aspect of article 9(1)(a).
46. The term “public security” is not defined in the AIE Regulations, the AIE Directive or the Aarhus Convention. The Aarhus Guide (p.86) explains: “The Convention does not define the terms “international relations”, “national defence” or “public security”, but it is implicit that the definition of such terms should be determined by the Parties in accordance with their generally accepted meaning in international law. Many national Governments already have similar exceptions in place and have interpreted them narrowly. Some countries have chosen to require information concerning the environment to be made publicly accessible, regardless of how it affects international relations, national defence or public security.”
47. I note that
Regulation (EU) 2018/1807
on a framework for the free flow of non-personal data in the European Union outlines, at Recital 19:
“The concept of ‘public security’, within the meaning of Article 52 TFEU and as interpreted by the Court of Justice, covers both the internal and external security of a Member State, as well as issues of public safety, in order, in particular, to facilitate the investigation, detection and prosecution of criminal offences. It presupposes the existence of a genuine and sufficiently serious threat affecting one of the fundamental interests of society, such as a threat to the functioning of institutions and essential public services and the survival of the population, as well as the risk of a serious disturbance to foreign relations or the peaceful coexistence of nations, or a risk to military interests. In compliance with the principle of proportionality, data localisation requirements that are justified on grounds of public security should be suitable for attaining the objective pursued, and should not go beyond what is necessary to attain that objective.” (emphasis added)
48. More recently, in Case C-106/22 Xella Magyarország Építőanyagipari Kft. v Innovációs és Technológiai Miniszter
, the CJEU noted that in the context of Article 52(1) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (which deals with derogations from EU fundamental freedoms), the requirements of public policy and public security must be interpreted strictly and “may be relied on only if there is a genuine and sufficiently serious threat to a fundamental interest of society.”
(paragraph 66).
49. In most cases, an analysis of public security involves an analysis of a specific risk of harm, for example a specific risk of harm to persons or property. In the decision in CEI/16/0041, my predecessor adopted this kind of analysis, examining whether the disclosure of the information “would lead to a direct or immediate threat to the security of the President”
, and concluding that it would not. However, it is now clear to me, from the judgment of the Supreme Court in the President’s case, that this focus on the physical security of the President was too narrow and failed to properly consider the fundamental nature of presidential immunity as part of the Irish constitutional order.
50. The Supreme Court’s judgment indicates that an interference with the constitutional immunity of the President is capable of having a more fundamental impact on ‘public security’, in the sense of amounting to a ‘genuine and serious threat to a fundamental interest of society’. The Court stated that the immunity of the President acknowledges and affords protection to the separation of powers (paragraph 96) and reflects a decision of the People to adopt a constitutional order that prevents the courts from engaging in any form of scrutiny of the exercise by the President of his or her powers (paragraph 97). The Court found:
“This makes the President different from those other organs of State which exercise political, legislative or administrative power. It does not merely mean that he is “above politics”, as I observed above, a commonly used phrase to describe the office of the President, but rather that it means that he or she stands constitutionally in a role which is sui generis and outside those structures which are amenable to court interference.” (paragraph 98)
51. The Court noted that the constitutional immunity for the President has been present since 1937 and long pre-dated the adoption of the AIE Directive, and that EU law permits the exclusion of a power of review where the Member State’s constitutional order so requires (paragraph 152).
52. I am satisfied that, throughout its judgment, the Supreme Court gave a very clear indication that to undermine presidential immunity would be to fundamentally undermine the Irish constitutional order. Taking into account the interpretation of ‘public security’ outlined in recital 19 to Regulation (EU) 2018/1807, as well as the judgment in Case C-106/22, I accept that, if the disclosure of information pursuant to an AIE request would undermine the constitutional immunity of the President, such disclosure would therefore adversely affect public security within the meaning of article 9(1)(a) of the AIE Regulations.
53. The question for me, therefore, is whether disclosure of the information requested in this case would undermine the constitutional immunity of the President.
54. The appellant is seeking access to: “ a record/spreadsheet/database of all air taxi services hired by the department on behalf of the President in 2023, 2024, 2025 to include the date, minute time on board, the route, the department, the number of passengers, and the cost of the service.”
In respect of air travel, the Department has indicated that the office of the President does not maintain an independent capacity to engage in air travel for official purposes, but instead relies on the Department to provide assistance. Had the President an independent capacity to engage in air travel (for example, had the President maintained his or her own air taxi service), any request for information about the President’s air travel would need to be made to the office of the President, which the Supreme Court has made clear is not permissible. As a result, I am satisfied that this request to the Department is, in effect, an indirect request to the President for environmental information and the Supreme Court has made it clear that “the immunity may not be avoided by a collateral request”
(paragraph 121).
55. I consider that distinction may be made between the situation in this case, where the Department holds the information based on the assistance it provides to the President in the exercise of presidential functions, and a situation where a public authority holds information that is generally about the President (for example, a briefing containing observations about a presidential event).
56. In my view, it is particularly relevant in this case that the President would be constitutionally unable to engage in proceedings before this Office. In the President
case, the appellant had argued that the Court should approach the President’s immunity narrowly, such that “the President could opt in or out of the process before the Commissioner, and could for example decline to answer at all, or give reasons for declining a request. He could, for example, have refused in the present case to furnish any information regarding his meetings with the Council of State by invoking his personal immunity, but it is argued that the President could as readily opt to furnish the information or engage with the Commissioner up to a point but not thereafter.”
The Court rejected this submission, noting that this would lead to a degree of uncertainty. The Court stated at paragraph 116:
“… the immunity operates not merely as a privilege conferred on the President, but also as a limitation on the court or the legislature engaging in acts of scrutiny. This immunity is a corollary to the prohibition of making the President answerable to either House of the Oireachtas or to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers and functions of his office under Article 13.8.1°, and as such the immunity cannot be waived or opted out of at the discretion of the President. The presidential immunity precludes the President making a choice to submit to the Commissioner and/or to a court, as the immunity must be seen as absolute in the sense that it has the effect of limiting scrutiny by the courts and is not a voluntarily assumed privilege but one inherent in the constitutional order.” (emphasis added)
57. The Court noted that the very purpose of the appeal to the High Court against the decision of this Office was to compel the President to furnish information to the requester, which no court could entertain, and continued: “The President was being put in the very dilemma from which the Constitution was meant to protect him: in order to defend himself and his position he would have to make himself answerable to a court or other authority.”
(paragraphs 118-119).
58. In this case, the request was made to the Department, but the information requested is information about the activities of a third party, the President. In a case involving the disclosure of potentially sensitive information of a third party, the third party has a right of appeal to this Office against a decision to release the information. Were the Department to release the requested information, the President would have a right of appeal, but one that could not be exercised by the President, as he or she does not have the option of making a choice to submit to the process of this Office, or to the process of the Court on appeal from a decision of this Office. This supports the conclusion that release of the requested information would be inconsistent with the constitutional immunity of the President.
59. In summary, I understand the Supreme Court’s judgment in the President
case to mean that the constitutional immunity of the President is of such fundamental importance to the Irish Constitution, that undermining it would adversely affect public security. Taking all of the above into account, I accept that the request for information in this case amounts to an indirect request to the President’s office for information concerning the exercise of presidential functions, the disclosure of which would undermine the constitutional immunity of the President. Accordingly, I accept that article 9(1)(a) applies in respect of the information sought.
Public Interest Test
60. I have found that article 9(1)(a) of the AIE Regulations applies in respect of the information sought. However, that is not the end of the matter. Article 10(3) of the AIE Regulations requires a public authority to consider each request on an individual basis and weigh the public interest served by disclosure against the interest served by refusal. Article 10(4) of the AIE Regulations provides that the grounds for refusal of a request shall be interpreted on a restrictive basis having regard to the public interest served by disclosure. Article 10(5) of the AIE Regulations provides that nothing in article 8 or 9 shall authorise a public authority not to make available environmental information which, although held with information to which article 8 or 9 relates, may be separated from such information.
61. In considering the public interest served by disclosure, I am mindful of the purpose of the AIE regime, as reflected in Recital 1 of the Preamble to the AIE Directive, which provides that “increased public access to environmental information and the dissemination of such information contribute to greater public awareness of environmental decision-making and, eventually, to a better environment.”
The AIE regime thereby recognises a very strong public interest in openness and transparency in relation to environmental decision-making. The AIE Regime also acknowledges that there may be exceptions to the general rule of disclosure of information, as noted in Recital 16 of the AIE Directive, which provides that “public authorities should be permitted to refuse a request for environmental information in specific and clearly defined cases.”
One such case is in respect of where disclosure would adversely affect international relations, national defence, or public security.
62. Taking into account the strong statements by the Supreme Court in the President
case, I am satisfied that the public interest in disclosure of the information would need to be very weighty indeed – exceptionally so – before it could outweigh any interference with the immunity of the President. The extent of the interference with immunity would also be relevant. For example, there may be a difference between a disclosure which could have a minimal, indirect impact on immunity and disclosure which clearly undermines the immunity. I have found above that the request in this case was, in effect, an indirect request to the President’s office for information in relation to the exercise of presidential functions, and that disclosure of this information would undermine the President’s immunity.
63. The information sought in this case concerns details of all air taxi services hired by the Department on behalf of the President in 2023, 2024, 2025 including the “date, minute time on board, the route, the department, the number of passengers, and the cost of the service.” While I accept that disclosure of this information would give general insight into aircraft usage by the President, I do not accept that the insight would be of such significant importance that it could outweigh the public interest in maintaining the constitutional immunity of the President. Accordingly, I find that the Department was justified under article 9(1)(a) of the AIE Regulations in refusing access to the information sought.
64. In accordance with article 10(5), I have considered whether the Department could have separated out information held with information to which article 9(1)(a) applies. Given that all of the information is interlinked and relates to the President, I am satisfied that it is appropriate to state that article 9(1)(a) applies to all of the information sought, and that the Department was unable to consider article 10(5) in this case.
65. Given my findings regarding article 9(1)(a) of the AIE Regulations, it is not necessary for me to consider the applicability of article 8(a)(ii) of the AIE Regulations.
Decision
66. Having carried out a review under article 12(5) of the AIE Regulations, I hereby affirm the Department’s decision, varying the basis. I find that the Department is a public authority in respect of the request, but I find that the Department was justified in refusing access to the information under article 9(1)(a) of the AIE Regulations.
Appeal to the High Court
67. A party to the appeal or any other person affected by this decision may appeal to the High Court on a point of law from the decision. Such an appeal must be initiated not later than two months after notice of the decision was given to the person bringing the appeal.
